To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have shown that computable distributions can be used to give semantics for a probabilistic programming language, and that this semantics is sound with respect to sampling-based semantics.

(i) we can give denotational and operational semantics to probabilistic functional languages that are based on computable probability distributions; and (ii) we can relate the denotational semantics of the language and its operational semantics.

1) we give denotitional semantics to a functional probabilistic language extended with continuous probability distributions and show that the semantics is compositional and 2) we give a sampling semantics to a functional programming language extended with continuous probabilities and show that it is equivalent to the denotational semantics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions.
the question of what it means for a program to have a distribution as a value.
a formalization of Bayesian inference in a functional language.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the paper presents a new approach to the semantics of probabilistic programming languages that combines operational and denotational approaches, and shows that the two can be related by restricting attention to a class of computable distributions.
computability theory can be used to give denotational and operational semantics to probabilistic programming languages.
we have provided a denotational semantics for the probabilistic functional language that is equivalent in power to the operational semantics, while being more precise and more general.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show how a probabilistic programming language with a denotational semantics can be given an operational semantics in terms sampling.

we have given semantics to a probabilistic programming language in the style of denotational semantics, which is then related to operational semantics by showing that computable distributions are exactly those distributions for which we can give an operational semantics.

we show that computable distributions are sufficient for the denotational semantics of the probabilistic language, and that they are also sufficient to give operational semantics in the form of sampling.
The main takeaway from our work is that
computability of distributions is a useful tool to bridge the gap between the operational and denotational approaches to the semantics of probabilistic programs.

we have shown how the semantics of a probabilistic programming language can be defined in terms of the computable distributions that are used to represent the probability distributions of the programs in the language.
computability is an important property of distributions in the semantics of probabilistic programming languages, and that we can use it to connect sampling semantics and denotational semantics.
